segments.title: Why destroyer-gun choices reveal doctrine
segments.body: A statistical ranking misses the central historical question because navies helped shape the weapons they selected. Caliber, mounting, loading arrangements, and rate of fire reflected how each service expected its destroyers to fight. The same gun could also serve destroyers, sloops, corvettes, or other escorts under different assumptions. National design priorities explain why navies accepted different compromises in their destroyer armament.

evidence.note: Navies developed gun characteristics around their expected methods of destroyer combat, across weapons also used by sloops and corvettes.

segments.summary: Destroyer-gun development followed each navy's expectations of combat, making doctrine essential to understanding the choice of weapons.

segments.title: Japan's 100 mm gun and the air-defense tradeoff
segments.body: Japan's 100 mm gun combined high elevation with rapid fire for fleet air defense. Its original 70-calibre design wore out too quickly, and the revised 65-calibre weapon entered service in 1942 after being designed in 1937. Ammunition supply normally held the firing rate near fifteen rounds per minute, with nineteen possible when the hoists worked well, despite higher theoretical figures for the breech mechanism. The mounting could elevate from minus 10 to plus 90 degrees. Its lighter shells were less effective against destroyers and larger surface targets, where rapid damage could stop an opponent from fighting back. Wider fitting as secondary armament on cruisers and capital ships would have strengthened Japanese air defense, while destroyers still needed enough shell power for surface combat.

evidence.note: The 100 mm gun combined unusually high elevation with a hoist-limited firing rate and modest surface shell effect, prompting a recommendation for wider use as fleet secondary armament.

segments.summary: Japan's high-angle 100 mm weapon offered excellent anti-aircraft performance but less surface punch for destroyer combat.

segments.title: Why torpedoes did not remove the need for destroyer gunfire
segments.body: A destroyer optimized for air defense still needed to damage surface opponents quickly. Torpedoes offered a powerful attack, but a missed salvo left the enemy able to continue fighting. Gunfire could progressively damage a target and inflict a mission kill by preventing it from fighting back. Japan's 100 mm weapon therefore involved a tradeoff: its anti-aircraft qualities did not provide the shell effect wanted against enemy destroyers or larger ships.

evidence.note: Gunfire could inflict progressive damage and prevent a target from fighting back, whereas a missed torpedo attack left the surface threat intact.

segments.summary: Gunfire could disable an opponent even without sinking it, giving destroyers a surface-combat requirement that torpedoes alone could not satisfy.

segments.title: Why the Royal Navy fielded so many 4-inch guns
segments.body: The Royal Navy retained large stocks of older guns and could adapt them faster than entirely new weapons could be produced. The Mark IX combined an earlier barrel with a different breech mechanism and entered service in 1917; roughly 2,400 were produced, leaving thousands available for the next war. Different 4-inch marks generally emphasized either surface or anti-aircraft work, with a secondary capability in the other role. They provided readily available armament for destroyers, frigates, corvettes, and reactivated ships. An older gun adapted in weeks could meet an immediate need while a better new weapon took a year or two to develop. Reusing old equipment exposed decision-makers to blame if it failed, so Britain often adopted the available weapon while developing its replacement. Shared caliber also concealed substantial differences between individual gun marks.

evidence.note: Britain's varied stocks of older 4-inch guns let the Royal Navy arm wartime ships quickly while newer weapons remained in development.

segments.summary: Britain's many 4-inch variants turned old stock, reserve weapons, and focused gun designs into immediately available wartime armament.

segments.title: The neglected US Navy 4-inch gun
segments.body: The American 4-inch Mark IX had entered service in 1914 and still fired only eight to nine rounds per minute without the sustained mechanical development given to British 4-inch weapons. Many flush-deck destroyers transferred to Britain were rearmed, usually with British guns, and transferred escort carriers also received replacement weapons. The old gun retained respectable armor penetration, but its handling and mechanisms had fallen behind. Those shortcomings reveal funding choices that fleet totals alone conceal. Flush-deck destroyers remained useful in secondary roles in 1942 and afterward, so their neglected armament continued to matter.

evidence.note: Interwar funding constraints left the capable American 4-inch gun without the sustained mechanical development needed to keep it current.

segments.summary: A capable First World War-era US gun became obsolete through neglect, exposing the hard funding choices beneath interwar fleet totals.

segments.title: Britain's 4.5-inch path to a true dual-purpose gun
segments.body: Admiral Reginald Henderson promoted a gun that could serve both high-angle and low-angle roles. Developing a suitable destroyer mounting proved harder than producing the gun and breech mechanism, because mounting weight and ammunition handling constrained the installation. Large ships provided room to use and develop the early equipment. Fixed ammunition proved too heavy to handle comfortably in rough conditions, prompting work on separate ammunition for destroyer use. Early twin mounts fired about twelve rounds per minute per gun, while later destroyer mounts reached fifteen to twenty. The time needed to improve the mounting and ammunition arrangements helped keep the 4.7-inch gun dominant in British destroyers until 1944.

evidence.note: Mounting weight and heavy fixed ammunition delayed wider destroyer use of the 4.5-inch family, while separate ammunition and improved mountings increased its practical value.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy's 4.5-inch family combined surface and anti-aircraft performance, but mounting weight and ammunition handling delayed destroyer adoption.

segments.title: The 4.5-inch Mark V: powered loading and barrel life
segments.body: The Mark V was designed in 1944 and officially entered service in 1947, placing most of its career after the war. An earlier prototype installation on a Battle-class destroyer brings its development into the wartime comparison. Power assistance allowed a designed rate of twenty-four rounds per minute. Hand operation generally produced twelve to fourteen rounds per minute, with bursts around eighteen, and the lower normal rate helped preserve barrel life. Crew fatigue and restricted turret space made mechanical assistance valuable even when the gun itself could cycle faster.

evidence.note: The Mark V's 1944 design and 1947 service date distinguish it from wartime predecessors, while powered operation, manual firing rates, and barrel preservation explain its practical performance.

segments.summary: The largely postwar Mark V shows how power assistance increased firing rate while routine operating limits protected barrel life.

segments.title: Swedish 120 mm guns for medium and neutral navies
segments.body: Bofors armed Swedish destroyers and exported related 120 mm designs to Polish and Dutch customers. Medium navies without a complete armaments industry could buy from Sweden without aligning closely with a major-power bloc. British spare-parts supplies carried political leverage, while American suppliers could restrict deliveries even in peacetime. Italy's reputation for rapid barrel wear and reservations about French metallurgy made those alternatives less attractive in this assessment. Limited American investment in gun development during the 1920s added another concern. Swedish weapons offered reliable service while reducing the political complications associated with buying from a great power.

evidence.note: Bofors offered Swedish, Polish, Dutch, and other medium navies a reliable procurement option outside the major political blocs.

segments.summary: Bofors gave medium navies a reliable 120 mm gun and a politically useful alternative to buying from a major-power bloc.

segments.title: How Swedish ships divided surface and air targets
segments.body: The 1924 and 1934 120 mm mounts elevated only to about 35 and 30 degrees, making them primarily surface-action weapons; the 1924 mounting was also entirely manual. Swedish planners paired these guns with 40 mm Bofors weapons for aircraft at shorter ranges. In a Baltic running fight against surface and air threats together, the lighter guns could take over nearby aircraft while the main battery returned to surface targets. The 1942 twin mounting's 80-degree elevation expanded the main battery's air-defense role after wartime experience exposed the limits of the earlier division.

evidence.note: Early Swedish low-angle 120 mm mounts handled surface targets while 40 mm Bofors guns covered nearby aircraft, until a high-angle twin mount expanded the main battery's role in 1942.

segments.summary: Low-angle 120 mm mounts and 40 mm Bofors guns divided the work of a Baltic running fight until the 1942 high-angle mounting expanded the main battery's anti-aircraft role.

segments.title: The 4.7-inch gun and British destroyer tactics
segments.body: Royal Navy destroyers were expected to fight through enemy screens and open opportunities for torpedo attacks. At night, fires started by shell hits on enemy capital ships could provide aiming points for torpedoes. The 4.7-inch weapon's shell effect, handling, and rate of fire served that surface doctrine very well. Its separated ammunition also eased manual handling during sustained surface action. Its mountings generally lacked the elevation and powered features needed for effective air defense under interwar displacement limits. Even the Mark 11 installation on the L and M classes reached only 50 degrees of elevation.

evidence.note: The British 4.7-inch gun suited close destroyer melees, screening, night fighting, and attacks that created openings for torpedoes.

segments.summary: Britain's 4.7-inch gun suited close destroyer actions, torpedo attacks, reconnaissance, and night fighting but was difficult to make fully dual purpose within treaty weights.

segments.title: How peacetime exercises distorted destroyer air defense
segments.body: Exercise incentives encouraged aircraft to attack carriers and battleships because simulated losses carried no mortal risk and high-value targets brought prestige. In war, exposed screening destroyers became much more attractive. Repeated exercises gave planners confidence in the same assumption, delaying serious attention to destroyer high-angle armament until Henderson and others challenged it. Repetition strengthened the group consensus without correcting the difference between simulated attacks and wartime risk.

evidence.note: Exercise pilots preferred prestigious capital-ship targets, creating misleading evidence that delayed British development of stronger destroyer air-defence mounts.

segments.summary: Peacetime pilots favored prestigious capital-ship targets, creating false evidence that destroyers would rarely face air attack.

segments.title: Why battleships versus carriers is a false interwar choice
segments.body: Enthusiasm for battleships did not necessarily imply opposition to aircraft carriers. British and American planners pursued both, retaining a mature striking weapon while developing naval aviation whose full capability had yet to arrive. Committing wholly to either type exposed national security to the risk of guessing wrongly about the pace of change. Italy's different approach grew out of bitter rivalry with its air force and confidence that bases around the peninsula and Mediterranean could cover the fleet.

evidence.note: Balanced interwar planning paired developing carriers with mature battleship forces, while Italian choices reflected inter-service rivalry and confidence in land-based air cover.

segments.summary: Interwar planners commonly pursued mature battleship power and developing naval aviation together rather than betting national security on only one system.

segments.title: The missed high-angle future of the British 4.7-inch
segments.body: The Royal Navy already had high-angle mountings and power rammers for some capital-ship installations, but did not turn that experience into its standard destroyer system. Treaty-driven weight savings and confidence in current surface performance kept the familiar mounts attractive. Small savings looked rational because planners believed the sacrificed air-defense capability would not matter. Reducing a Tribal-style battery to six guns could have released weight for powered high-angle mountings.

evidence.note: Existing high-angle mountings and power rammers supported a proposed six-gun destroyer arrangement that traded gun count for more capable mounts.

segments.summary: Existing high-angle 4.7-inch technology suggests Britain could have traded gun count for a stronger dual-purpose destroyer mounting.

segments.title: How Ansaldo and OTO competed over Italy's 120 mm guns
segments.body: Italian manufacturers developed a succession of related 120 mm guns during the 1920s and 1930s. OTO and Ansaldo repeatedly answered one another's models, building on a lineage that included Schneider-Canet-Armstrong and Vickers-Terni designs. The Schneider-Canet-Armstrong Model 1918 supplied the starting point, followed by the Vickers-Terni Model 1924 and OTO Model 1926. Ansaldo's 120 mm/50 response began another round of competition. These developments served a naval requirement for decisive hits in the confined Adriatic, where nearby opponents threatened Italy's expected control of its home waters.

evidence.note: Italy's Adriatic requirement shaped a sequence of related 120 mm designs from Schneider-Canet-Armstrong, Vickers-Terni, OTO, and Ansaldo.

segments.summary: Italian firms repeatedly answered one another's 120 mm designs, developing a gun family around the navy's demand for hard-hitting weapons in the Adriatic.

segments.title: Italy's 120 mm choice: velocity over rate of fire
segments.body: Early variants managed roughly six to seven rounds per minute because their breech and loading arrangements slowed the crews. Contemporary British Tribal-class guns could manage about ten to twelve rounds per minute with shells of similar weight. The Italian guns traded firing volume for a muzzle velocity near 3,000 feet per second, promising penetration and kinetic effect when a shell landed. This choice prioritized making each hit count over putting the greatest possible number of shells into the air. It also matched an expectation of surface engagements in Mediterranean and Adriatic conditions that were generally more stable than the North Atlantic.

evidence.note: Italian 120 mm guns traded breech speed and practical rate of fire for high muzzle velocity suited to expected Mediterranean conditions.

segments.summary: Italian 120 mm development favored high velocity and decisive shell effect for Mediterranean and Adriatic combat, accepting slower mechanisms and a lower practical rate of fire.

segments.title: Dutch Bofors guns for East Indies operations
segments.body: Dutch requirements emphasized an all-round weapon for destroyers, sloops, and gunboats that might face attack while operating independently in the East Indies. Shorter barrels, powered loading, and stabilized mounting designs aimed to improve anti-aircraft use while retaining surface capability. The planned Mark 9 for the 1938 gunboats and battlecruisers would have reached 80 degrees of elevation. Most other mounts reached only 45 or 55 degrees, leaving restrictions similar to those of British destroyer installations. Limited production and the absence of the planned battlecruiser installation make the design's full potential difficult to judge.

evidence.note: Dutch 120 mm development sought powered loading and stabilization, but most mounts reached only 45 or 55 degrees against the planned Mark 9's 80 degrees.

segments.summary: The Dutch adapted Swedish 120 mm designs toward higher elevation, stabilization, and self-defense for ships operating independently in the East Indies.

segments.title: Why the 5-inch/38 succeeded as a complete system
segments.body: The 5-inch/38's strength lay in the combination of gun, powered mounting, ammunition supply, and fire control. High elevation and rapid loading at all angles supported fire against ships and aircraft. Fast handoffs also reduced the time crews spent holding heavy ammunition, helping them sustain their work. American development treated these components as a system early enough for the gun to enter service in 1934 and its initial troubles to be resolved quickly. In this assessment, the British 4.5-inch gun had a slight anti-shipping edge once it used separate ammunition. That advantage was too small to outweigh the performance of the complete American installation.

evidence.note: Hoists, loading arrangements, fire control, and crew endurance made the complete 5-inch/38 installation exceptional beyond the gun itself.

segments.summary: The 5-inch/38's claim to be the best all-round destroyer weapon rests on its complete installation, including the mounting, ammunition supply, and fire control.

segments.title: Why the 5-inch/38 needed a new barrel design
segments.body: The US Navy wanted to retain its familiar 5-inch caliber while improving surface firepower and air defense. The 5-inch/38 design dated to 1932 and entered service in 1934, replacing reliance on the older 5-inch/51. Its shorter barrel gave greater flexibility and reduced weight. Improved metallurgy and design also mattered: simply shortening a 5-inch/51 barrel by 65 inches would still have left it heavier than the new barrel.

evidence.note: The 1932 design and 1934 service dates, shorter barrel, and further weight saving from improved metallurgy distinguish the 5-inch/38 from merely shortening a 5-inch/51.

segments.summary: The 5-inch/38 retained a familiar caliber while reducing barrel length and weight for more flexible surface and anti-aircraft use.

segments.title: Germany's 127 mm gun and the deployment gap
segments.body: Germany's 127 mm gun had a quoted rate of fifteen to eighteen rounds per minute, conditional on calm water and a well-trained crew. Those qualifications exposed the gap between a theoretical firing rate and performance from a moving destroyer. The manually controlled 1934 mount reached only 30 degrees of elevation, while the 1938 version improved that to 40 degrees. A theoretical 360-degree traverse was further restricted by the mounting's position on the hull. These limits left the weapon poorly suited to air defense compared with the American 5-inch/38 installation. In this assessment, they reflected a navy whose practical development still lagged after the contraction imposed by Versailles.

evidence.note: Calm-water and crew-training requirements limited the weapon's rate of fire, while restricted mount performance reflected Germany's naval rebuilding gap.

segments.summary: Germany's nominally rapid 127 mm destroyer gun was constrained by manual, low-elevation mounts and a force still rebuilding practical naval capability.

segments.title: Why advanced doctrine did not mean a fully modernized force
segments.body: German forces could promote advanced ideas about mechanized warfare without being able to motorize the whole army. The British Army had largely motorized by the beginning of World War II, although some reserve formations were still converting. Pack animals remained useful for mountain warfare, particularly in the Indian Army. The comparison connects Germany's uneven army modernization with a naval force still overcoming the contraction imposed after World War I. In this assessment, practical deployment lagged behind promising theory.

evidence.note: German limits on army motorization are compared with British conversion and the continued use of pack animals in mountain warfare, illustrating the gap between advanced ideas and practical deployment.

segments.summary: Germany's interest in mechanized warfare exceeded its ability to motorize the whole army, a comparison that helps explain the practical shortcomings of its naval rebuilding.

segments.title: Japan's 127 mm guns and attrition doctrine
segments.body: Japanese strategy treated decisive battle as the endpoint after successive torpedo and escort attacks had worn an approaching fleet down. The Type 89 had a claimed initial rate of fourteen rounds per minute, falling nearer eight once ready ammunition was exhausted and the supply chain took over. A rate of fourteen rounds per minute might be achieved on land by an exceptional crew, but appears unrealistic at sea with this loading arrangement. Fitted to capital ships, carriers, cruisers, and Matsu- and Tachibana-class escorts, the weapon helped reveal what Japan required from a high-angle fleet gun.

evidence.note: A claimed fourteen rounds per minute for the Type 89 dropped to eight sustained once its ammunition supply became the bottleneck. The peak figure is doubted at sea. Japanese doctrine combined repeated attacks and long-range torpedo hits with attrition before a final decisive battle.

segments.summary: The Type 89's ammunition bottleneck illustrates how Japan's 127 mm weapons served an attritional route toward decisive battle rather than a single isolated fleet clash.

segments.title: Why elevation alone did not make Japan's 127 mm gun effective
segments.body: The Third Year Type 127 mm armed Fubuki and many later Japanese destroyer classes through several single and twin mountings. Depending on the mounting, maximum elevation was about 55 or 75 degrees, while quoted firing rates ranged from roughly five to ten rounds per minute. Mount selection reflected weight limits, expected operations, and differing assessments of air-attack risk. The high-angle versions could throw shells to roughly 40,000 feet, but the targeting system could not turn that reach alone into accurate anti-aircraft fire. Better investment in the supporting system could have made these widely distributed guns more useful across the fleet.

evidence.note: Third Year Type mount variants traded weight and elevation, with inadequate targeting support limiting the usefulness of their high-angle reach.

segments.summary: Japan's Third Year Type 127 mm mounts could reach aircraft altitudes, but high elevation needed suitable fire control to become effective anti-aircraft capability.

segments.title: How destroyer hull strength affected gun accuracy
segments.body: Fubuki's reinforcement in 1936 illustrates how hull construction affected the performance of the weapons above it. Japanese interwar designs pursued low structural weight to fit more capability within treaty tonnage. American destroyer design placed greater emphasis on seaworthiness after experience with flush-deck destroyers, while speed strongly influenced Italian and French hulls. A light hull had less capacity to withstand repeated firing at different angles. Underwater damage could also distort the deck, disturbing gun stability, control, and accuracy. The gun's performance therefore depended partly on how its hull carried firing loads and survived damage.

evidence.note: Fubuki's reinforcement, contrasting national hull priorities, and the effects of repeated firing and damage-induced distortion on gun accuracy and stability.

segments.summary: Lightweight hulls could distort under firing loads or damage, affecting gun accuracy and control; Fubuki's reinforcement shows why hull strength mattered.

segments.title: French 130 mm guns and the first-hit philosophy
segments.body: French destroyer design emphasized hitting hard at the first opportunity, especially against Italian forces in the Mediterranean. Limited fleet numbers and treaty parity with Italy encouraged an interest in heavy guns that could also threaten cruisers. The 1919 model managed about four to five rounds per minute and the 1924 model five to six, while the 1935 model could reach ten to fifteen depending on the crew and circumstances. Ammunition endurance remained a constraint: the later destroyer carried about 170 rounds per gun, against 400 on Dunkerque and a British norm near 300. Speed and firepower took priority over the stores needed for prolonged operations far from supply. French concern about the Far East reached ship design and sustainment planning later than its Mediterranean requirements.

evidence.note: French first-hit thinking favored hard-hitting 130 mm guns. Later models improved the firing rate, but smaller destroyer ammunition stocks and limited Far East sustainment planning constrained endurance.

segments.summary: France sought heavier destroyer shells to compensate for limited numbers, improving firing rates across successive models while accepting smaller ammunition stocks.

segments.title: Why France's 138.6 mm destroyer gun underdelivered
segments.body: The large weapon promised decisive shell effect against destroyers and cruisers. The 1929 model could reach twelve rounds per minute but normally fired about seven, while the 1934 model managed five to nine. A destroyer lacked the turret space, machinery allowance, crew room, and ammunition capacity that let a true light cruiser sustain fire from comparable guns. Mounts limited to 30 degrees of elevation and magazines of roughly 100 rounds per gun further reduced its value as an all-purpose weapon. A proposed alternative was a small cruiser with enough space for a true dual-purpose mounting, able to act as an anti-aircraft, surface-action, or picket ship. That remained a hypothetical use for a weapon compromised in the contre-torpilleur form.

evidence.note: France's 138.6 mm destroyer gun approached cruiser shell power, but limited space, rate of fire, elevation, and magazine capacity prevented a destroyer from using it like a cruiser.

segments.summary: France put near-cruiser firepower into destroyer hulls, but cramped mounts, low elevation, and small magazines prevented the 138.6 mm gun from realizing its paper advantage.

segments.title: Germany's 150 mm destroyers as a failed cruiser shortcut
segments.body: Germany had already fitted 150 mm weapons to some large torpedo boats and submarines during World War I, and their breech design influenced France's 1927 model of the 138.6 mm gun. The later German 150 mm destroyers sought to offset shortages of cruisers and create dedicated destroyer killers. The same approach ran through the force structure: ocean-going torpedo boats were expected to approximate destroyers while 150 mm destroyers were expected to approximate light cruisers. The heavy forward mounting worsened seakeeping, and practical rates of fire fell below paper claims. The twin mount's stated 65-degree elevation offered some potential for air defense, while the single mounts reached only 30 degrees. Low firing rates and ammunition stowage of about 120 rounds per gun further limited usefulness. Battles such as Narvik showed why destroyer fights tended to become close-range sea dogfights. A fully dual-purpose 127 mm mounting would have offered a more useful balance of elevation, firing rate, and surface capability.

evidence.note: Earlier German 150 mm breeches influenced French gun development. The later German destroyers tried to substitute for light cruisers, but handling, ammunition capacity, and low-angle single mounts limited their usefulness.

segments.summary: Six-inch-class guns could not turn a destroyer hull into a light cruiser and performed poorly in the close, violent conditions of destroyer combat.

segments.title: What large destroyers were expected to do for different navies
segments.body: Britain, France, Italy, and Germany all faced choices between a large destroyer and a small cruiser. British and Italian solutions retained destroyer armament in larger ships. Britain's Tribal class also borrowed a cruiser-like appearance: the interrupted line of portholes suggested an armor belt, especially when seen at night. The British requirement emphasized diplomatic presence and reconnaissance, while French and Italian requirements reflected their Mediterranean rivalry. Germany expected its heavily armed destroyers to kill enemy destroyers and help cover the shortage of light cruisers. Their destroyer hulls and stability still limited how effectively they could fight as cruisers.

evidence.note: Different national requirements for large destroyers, including Tribal-class appearance and diplomatic or reconnaissance work, Mediterranean rivalry, and Germany's attempt to cover a shortage of cruisers.

segments.summary: Britain's Tribal class filled diplomatic and reconnaissance roles, while German large destroyers were expected to compensate for a shortage of light cruisers.

segments.title: Why wartime shipbuilding made destroyers the mass threat
segments.body: A destroyer could be built and commissioned in roughly eighteen months, while a cruiser needed about two to two and a half years and larger ships demanded still more resources. More yards could construct destroyers, so wartime mobilization naturally increased their numbers fastest. Their low profiles, high speed, and movement in rough water also shortened visual engagement ranges. Those conditions favored rapid, flexible gun systems for close fights rather than oversized weapons optimized for long-range duels.

evidence.note: Shorter construction times and wider yard capacity made destroyers the growing wartime threat, while low visibility and rough-water movement drove their battles toward close range.

segments.summary: Destroyers could be built faster and in more yards than cruisers or capital ships, making them the surface opponent wartime fleets were most likely to meet in growing numbers.

segments.title: The decisive advantage was the whole gun system
segments.body: Treaty limitations helped shape differences among American, British, and Japanese destroyer designs. The concluding design problem gives every navy its preferred gun in a fully dual-purpose mounting, with elevation up to 85 degrees. Powered assistance allows loading and firing at any angle, matching the support offered by the American 5-inch/38 system. The question remains open: how would World War II change if every navy had that standard of gun installation?

evidence.note: The closing counterfactual asks how each navy would fare with an equivalent powered dual-purpose mounting system and leaves the answer open.

segments.summary: The closing counterfactual asks how World War II changes if every navy pairs its preferred gun with powered loading, high elevation, and integrated support comparable to the 5-inch/38 system.
